name: Libertarianism
info: Libertarianism is a political philosophy that holds negative liberty and personal sovereignty as primary values; it began as a left-wing anti-state politics in the mid-19th century and took its best-known form as a revival of classical liberalism in the United States.

facts.thinkers: John Locke, whose Two Treatises of Government (1689) set out liberal political theory; William Godwin, who took liberalism to an anarchic conclusion; Joseph Déjacque, the first to call himself a libertarian; H. L. Mencken and Albert Jay Nock, the first prominent Americans to use the word as a synonym for liberal; Murray Rothbard, who popularised the term in its American sense; Robert Nozick, who argued for a minimal state; Hillel Steiner and Peter Vallentyne among left-libertarians
facts.texts: Locke’s Two Treatises of Government (1689); Godwin’s Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (1793); Isabel Paterson’s The God of the Machine, Rose Wilder Lane’s The Discovery of Freedom and Ayn Rand’s The Fountainhead (all 1943); Georges Fontenis’s Manifesto of Libertarian Communism (1953); Nozick’s Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974); Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein’s Nudge
facts.ideas: negative liberty and personal sovereignty; the non-aggression principle; equality before the law and civil rights; spontaneous order; private property and self-ownership (for right-libertarians); common ownership of natural resources (for left-libertarians); opposition to militarism and a foreign policy of non-interventionism
facts.today: Libertarian parties exist in the United States, the United Kingdom, Israel, South Africa, Argentina and other countries; the Libertarian Party of the United States was formed in 1971; in 2023 Javier Milei was elected in Argentina as the first self-identified libertarian head of state; libertarian socialists point to the Zapatista territory in Chiapas and the Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria

t: Libertarianism holds negative liberty and personal sovereignty as primary values, and many libertarians connect freedom with the non-aggression principle: each person may live as they choose so long as they do not initiate force or fraud against others.

The word was first used for a new set of political positions by Joseph Déjacque in 1857, when libertarianism was a form of anarchist or left-wing politics; in the mid-20th century American proponents of free markets took it up, and it came to be widely associated with the right.

Scholars sort libertarians along left–right or socialist–capitalist lines by their views of property and capital: right-libertarians defend private property in land and the means of production, left-libertarians hold natural resources to belong to everyone or to be owned collectively.
dyk: Libertarian was already in print in 1796, when the London Packet reported 450 “French Libertarians” marching out of the prison at Bristol, and there it meant a supporter of republicanism.
ev: John Locke’s Two Treatises of Government sets out the basis of liberal political theory
Joseph Déjacque calls himself a libertarian in a letter to Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
The Spanish Revolution brings libertarian socialism its greatest popularity
Paterson, Lane and Rand each publish a book promoting individualism and capitalism
Leonard E. Read founds the Foundation for Economic Education
A small group led by David Nolan forms the Libertarian Party
Robert Nozick publishes Anarchy, State, and Utopia
Javier Milei is elected president of Argentina at the head of the La Libertad Avanza coalition

sections.origins:
Elements of libertarianism have been traced to the higher-law concepts of the Greeks and the Israelites and to Christian theologians who divided the world into two realms, one beyond the power of states. David Boaz of the Cato Institute notes that Laozi advocated for rulers to “do nothing”. Scholastic thinkers including Thomas Aquinas, Francisco de Vitoria and Bartolomé de Las Casas argued for “self-mastery” as the foundation of individual rights. In 17th-century England libertarian ideas took modern form in the writings of the Levellers and John Locke, whose Two Treatises of Government (1689) held that people’s rights existed before government, that its purpose is to protect personal and property rights, and that people may dissolve governments that fail to do so.

The word is older than the doctrine. As early as 1796 libertarian meant a defender of liberty and a supporter of republicanism. Its use for a new set of political positions has been traced to the French libertaire, coined in a letter by the libertarian communist Joseph Déjacque to Pierre-Joseph Proudhon in 1857; Déjacque also named his anarchist journal Le Libertaire, printed in New York City from 1858 to 1861. Libertarianism began as an anti-authoritarian, anti-state politics usually seen as on the left.

In the United States in the mid-20th century the word was taken up by classical liberals. H. L. Mencken and Albert Jay Nock were the first prominent figures to call themselves libertarian, believing that Franklin D. Roosevelt had taken the word liberal for his New Deal policies. According to David Boaz, three books of 1943 gave birth to the modern libertarian movement, though none of their authors used the term.
sections.ideas:
Libertarianism holds negative liberty and personal sovereignty as primary values. Many libertarians connect freedom with the non-aggression principle, under which each individual may live as they choose as long as they do not violate others’ rights by initiating force or fraud. Libertarians emphasise equality before the law and civil rights, among them freedom of association, speech, thought and choice, and they generally oppose state power, warfare, militarism and nationalism. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines libertarianism as the moral view that agents initially fully own themselves and have certain moral powers to acquire property rights in external things.

Libertarians argue that some forms of order emerge spontaneously from the actions of many individuals without central planning, and they name language and a free market economy among the examples. What libertarianism means is contentious even among libertarians. Right-libertarianism, based on the works of Locke, Frédéric Bastiat, Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises, values institutions that support capitalist conditions. Anarcho-capitalists seek the replacement of the state by privately funded security services, while minarchists defend night-watchman states limited to protecting natural rights.

Left-libertarians such as Hillel Steiner, Peter Vallentyne, Philippe Van Parijs, Michael Otsuka and David Ellerman hold that natural resources belong to everyone, and that appropriation of land must leave “enough and as good” for others or be taxed to compensate them. Socialist libertarians criticise the state as the defender of private property and hold that capitalism entails wage slavery.
sections.spread:
The libertarian socialist strand spread through the anarchist movement. A French anarchist congress used the term libertarian communism in November 1880, according to Max Nettlau, and Sébastien Faure began a weekly Le Libertaire in 1895. In the early 20th century libertarian communism and anarchist communism became synonymous, especially through their close connection in Spain. Georges Fontenis wrote the Manifesto of Libertarian Communism in 1953 for the Federation Communiste Libertaire of France, and the Libertarian League was founded in New York City in 1954. In Australia the Sydney Push, a left-wing intellectual subculture, was associated with the label Sydney libertarianism from the late 1940s to the early 1970s.

In the United States the free-market strand grew from the Foundation for Economic Education, founded by Leonard E. Read in 1946, and from the journal Left and Right (1965–1968), founded by Karl Hess and Murray Rothbard with others. The Vietnam War split the alliance between libertarians and conservatives who believed in limiting liberty to uphold moral virtues. Some libertarians joined the draft resistance and peace movements, and in 1969 and 1970 two conferences brought together the New Left and the Old Right; Rothbard later broke with the left and allied himself with the paleoconservative movement.

Since the 1970s this classical liberal form of libertarianism has spread beyond the United States through think tanks and parties, which were established in the United Kingdom, Israel, South Africa, Argentina and many other countries. Variants include libertarian paternalism, advanced by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein in Nudge, neo-libertarianism, first described by James Sterba in 1980, and libertarian populism.
sections.power:
The record of libertarians is mostly one of parties, elections and movements. In 1971 a small group led by David Nolan formed the Libertarian Party. In 1975 Ronald Reagan, then governor of California, told Reason he believed “the very heart and soul of conservatism is libertarianism”, and Ron Paul supported his 1980 campaign. Libertarians later criticised Reagan: Paul recalled being the only Republican to vote against Reagan’s budget proposals in 1981, and Rothbard called Reagan’s presidency “a disaster for libertarianism in the United States”.

The Tea Party movement of 2009 had a significant libertarian component, and a 2011 Reason-Rupe poll found that 41 percent of its supporters leaned libertarian. In 2012 the Libertarian Party nominated Gary Johnson, who received more than 1.2 million votes, about 1 percent; in 2016 Johnson received more than 4.3 million votes, about 3 percent, the best result in the party’s history by vote number. After the 2022 convention the Mises Caucus, a paleolibertarian faction, became the dominant faction on the party’s national committee.

In Argentina, Javier Milei, a self-described “liberal libertarian”, won the 2023 general election as leader of La Libertad Avanza and was described as the first self-identified libertarian head of state; his proposals included large cuts in government spending and the elimination of numerous federal agencies. Libertarian socialists point to the Spanish Revolution of 1936, in which means of production were brought under workers’ control, and to the Zapatista territory in Chiapas and the Rojava Revolution in Syria. Liberals and communists blamed the libertarian socialists for the defeat of the Spanish Republic, a charge Robin Hahnel and Noam Chomsky dispute.
sections.critiques:
Criticism of libertarianism includes ethical, economic, environmental, pragmatic and philosophical concerns. It is most often voiced by critics on the left and aimed at the more right-leaning schools. One argument is that libertarianism lacks an explicit theory of liberty: if liberty is the absence of constraint, it is hard to decide which rights prevail when they conflict. Others argue that laissez-faire capitalism does not necessarily produce the best or most efficient outcome and that deregulation does not prevent abuse of natural resources. Critics have accused libertarians of an “atomistic” individualism that ignores the role of communities; libertarians reply that they oppose only forced communal ties.

Corey Robin describes this type of libertarianism as a reactionary conservative ideology joined to traditionalist conservatism by a desire to enforce hierarchical power and social relations. Nancy MacLean argues that it is a radical right ideology that has stood against democracy, and that Charles and David Koch used campaign contributions, a network of institutes and lobbying for libertarian, pro-business judges to oppose taxes, public education, employee protection laws and environmental protection laws. The conservative philosopher Russell Kirk wrote that libertarians “bear no authority, temporal or spiritual”; libertarians answer that they do venerate ancient traditions but oppose using law to force others to follow them.

Libertarians dispute one another as well. Right-libertarians such as Rothbard and Hoppe argue that libertarian socialism’s rejection of private property in the means of production relies on coercion, and the anarchist scholar Simon Critchley calls contemporary neoliberalism a “pseudo-libertarianism”.
sections.legacy:
Modern libertarianism gained recognition in academia with Robert Nozick’s Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), which won a National Book Award in 1975. Written in response to John Rawls’s A Theory of Justice, it argued for a minimal state on the ground that an ultraminimal state arises without violating individual rights. Through Nozick the term spread in academic and philosophical circles outside the United States.

The project of spreading libertarian ideals in the United States has been so successful that some Americans who do not call themselves libertarian seem to hold libertarian views. Gallup polls of 2015 put the figure of libertarian-leaning voters at 27 percent, and a Reuters poll that year found 23 percent of American voters self-identifying as libertarian; a 2014 Pew poll found that 11 percent both identified as libertarians and understood the term. Libertarian typology is often drawn on a two-dimensional chart such as the Nolan Chart, culturally liberal and fiscally conservative, favouring legalised victimless crimes, lower taxes and non-interventionism. The Free State Project, founded in 2001, recruited libertarians to move to New Hampshire, where about 6,232 participants had moved by May 2022.

Elsewhere the word still often means anarchism or libertarian socialism, and the free-market form is often called liberalism, for example in Europe. After the fall of the Soviet Union libertarian socialism grew in influence alongside anti-globalisation movements, and Gabriel Boric, a self-described libertarian socialist, became president of Chile in 2022.

summary: Libertarianism is a political philosophy built on negative liberty, personal sovereignty and the non-aggression principle. It began in the 19th century as a left-wing anti-state politics, and in the mid-20th century American free-market thinkers made the word their own, so that left and right schools now differ over property and capital.
